issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: Military-themed conversations are hard to reconcile with a life-threatening illness trauma in a 51-year-old school principal; this trigger implies a combat-related context not represented anywhere else in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar People: Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar
issues.explanation: Avoiding people involved in the event or who look similar fits interpersonal/assault/accident traumas better than life-threatening illness, where there are typically no 'other people involved' in that sense. It is not well supported by the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Future Orientation: Talking about the future
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'talking about the future' as a trigger is plausible, but 'alcohol smell' is hard to connect unless alcohol was part of treatment context; nothing else in the profile supports that association, making this trigger set clinically incoherent.

'People can't be trusted' is more typical of interpersonal trauma and is poorly anchored to a life-threatening illness trauma in the absence of any treatment-related betrayal, conflict, or mistrust themes elsewhere in the profile.

'Crying' is not a trauma cue but an affective response/behavior, so it is clinically incoherent as a trigger item relative to the other trigger items, which are concrete sensory reminders linked to life-threatening illness (alcohol smell, hospital/antiseptic smell).

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted
issues.explanation: A global mistrust appraisal is a poor fit for the rest of the profile and trauma type. In life-threatening illness, the other items center on altered self and self-reliance, while 'People can't be trusted' implies an interpersonal betrayal/threat theme that is not supported by the memory, trigger, or strategy items and does not align well with the otherwise weak/inactive Threat links.

vignette: Ryan's eyes scanned the empty halls of his school, a familiar sense of dread settling in as he caught a whiff of disinfectant. It was a smell that transported him back to the hospital, where just over a year ago, he had spent weeks fighting for his life against a relentless illness. The scent was overpowering, and Ryan's mind began to reel as memories long suppressed threatened to surface. He knew what would happen if he let those memories take hold – the same debilitating anxiety that had taken over his life since the hospital stay would kick in, rendering him unable to function. So, he did what he always did: rehearsed conversations with staff members, mentally preparing himself for every possible scenario, a desperate attempt to regain control. He also avoided going near the school nurse's office, fearing any reminders of medical procedures might trigger another episode. The irony wasn't lost on Ryan – as a principal, he was expected to be a pillar of strength, yet his own body had betrayed him in ways he couldn't shake off. Some days, it felt like his memories were fragmented and inaccessible, while others brought the full emotional intensity without any clear image or recollection. There were moments when his body would involuntarily contort into the same position as during those harrowing hospital days, sending him spiraling back. The hardest part for Ryan was recognizing himself in this new reality – he had become unrecognizable to himself, unable to rely on his own judgment or trust his body. His entire identity was now intertwined with feelings of inadequacy and self-doubt. When these thoughts consumed him, Ryan cut off contact with friends and family, further isolating himself from the world. The vicious cycle fed itself – Ryan's desperate attempts to regain control by rehearsing conversations only led to increased anxiety when he inevitably failed to predict every outcome. His memories, fragmented and painful as they were, reinforced his conviction that he couldn't trust himself or his body. This distrust fueled more avoidance behaviors, particularly around medical settings. Recently, Ryan had caught a glimpse of an ambulance outside the school – its sirens silent but menacing – and something inside him snapped. He realized he needed help breaking free from this self-perpetuating nightmare, even if it meant confronting those unbearable memories head-on. The hardest part would be admitting to others that he, the once-strong principal, was no longer in control of his own life. As Ryan navigated these treacherous waters, a glimmer of hope flickered – maybe with help, he could find a way to reconcile this shattered self and rebuild trust in himself and his body.
